relations.myth: Umā reveals the vanished yakṣa as Brahman
relations.note: She identifies Brahman as the true source of the gods’ victory.

relations.myth: Umā teaches Indra who won the gods’ victory
relations.note: She reveals that Brahman, not the gods, achieved their victory.
She is Śiva’s dominant consort throughout epic, Purāṇic and Śaiva traditions.

relations.myth: Pārvatī serves Śiva during his meditation
relations.note: She attends the meditating Śiva before undertaking her own austerities.

relations.myth: Śiva tests Pārvatī while disguised as an ascetic
relations.note: She defends Śiva against his disguised criticism and proves her constancy.

relations.myth: Śiva and Pārvatī play dice
relations.note: Their game becomes a dispute over possessions, pride or illusion.

relations.myth: Pārvatī merges bodily with Śiva as Ardhanārīśvara
relations.note: Their divided composite body expresses inseparable Śiva and Śakti.

relations.myth: Annapūrṇā feeds the food-denying Śiva
relations.note: As Annapūrṇā, she feeds Śiva and demonstrates matter’s indispensability.
Epic and Purāṇic traditions make her the mountain-god’s daughter.

relations.myth: The supreme Goddess teaches Himavat
relations.note: Śākta theology presents the Goddess teaching her nominal mountain father.
She is the younger daughter of Menā and Himavat.
The Rāmāyaṇa names Gaṅgā the elder and Umā the younger sister.

relations.myth: Gaṅgā carries Śiva’s energy toward Skanda’s birth
relations.note: They share Skanda’s distributed maternity, with Gaṅgā carrying Śiva’s generative energy.

relations.myth: Pārvatī resents Gaṅgā dwelling in Śiva’s hair
relations.note: Later Gaṅgādhara folklore portrays the sisters as rivals for Śiva.
Developed genealogies call her the sister of the mountain Maināka.

relations.myth: Satī is reborn as Himavat’s daughter Pārvatī
relations.note: Purāṇic synthesis identifies Pārvatī as Śiva’s first wife reborn.
Through her identity as Satī reborn, Pārvatī is Dakṣa’s daughter.

relations.myth: Satī confronts Dakṣa at his sacrifice
relations.note: As Satī, she condemns her father’s abuse of Śiva and destroys her body.
She is his mother, foster-mother or claimant, depending on the birth tradition.

relations.myth: Agni carries Śiva’s energy toward Skanda’s birth
relations.note: Agni transports Śiva’s generative energy after the gods interrupt the couple.

relations.myth: The Kṛttikās nurse Skanda
relations.note: Pārvatī accepts or recovers the child fostered by the Kṛttikās.

relations.myth: Svāhā shares Skanda’s dispersed maternity
relations.note: Mahābhārata variants include Svāhā among the figures involved in Skanda’s birth.

relations.myth: Competing traditions name each goddess Murukaṉ’s mother
relations.note: Tamil tradition gives Koṟṟavai an alternative maternity later assimilated to Pārvatī’s family.

relations.myth: Pārvatī creates Gaṇeśa from her bodily substance
relations.note: She fashions him while bathing and appoints him guardian of her door.
Other traditions make him the naturally or miraculously born son of the couple.

relations.myth: Pārvatī demands restoration of beheaded Gaṇeśa
relations.note: Her threat of cosmic destruction compels Śiva to restore her son.

relations.myth: Pārvatī produces Aśokasundarī from a wish-fulfilling tree
relations.note: A less widely attested tradition makes Aśokasundarī her created daughter.

relations.myth: Andhaka is entrusted to the divine couple
relations.note: Some accounts make Pārvatī an adoptive guardian; others leave Andhaka unrelated.

relations.myth: Kāma tries awakening Śiva’s desire for Pārvatī
relations.note: Kāma intervenes on her behalf, but Śiva burns him with his third eye.

relations.myth: Pārvatī helps occasion Kāma’s restoration
relations.note: Some later narratives associate her with restoring Rati’s burned husband as Ananga.

relations.myth: Brahmā officiates at Pārvatī’s wedding
relations.note: He performs or attends her marriage and supports the plan for Śiva’s son.

relations.myth: Viṣṇu participates in Pārvatī’s divine wedding
relations.note: He attends the marriage and joins the gods’ plan for Śiva’s son.

relations.myth: Viṣṇu gives Pārvatī away as her ritual brother
relations.note: Some regional wedding rites appoint Viṣṇu her brother without asserting universal genealogy.

relations.myth: Nārada advises Pārvatī to undertake tapas
relations.note: Purāṇic versions make him announce her destiny or counsel her austerities.

relations.myth: Nārada provokes divine family contests
relations.note: He instigates disputes and competitions within Pārvatī’s household in later narratives.

relations.myth: Nandin joins the divine wedding and household
relations.note: Śiva’s attendant participates in Pārvatī’s wedding and family episodes.

relations.myth: Pārvatī seeks a guard independent of Śiva’s attendants
relations.note: His loyalty to Śiva helps motivate her creation of Gaṇeśa.

relations.myth: Pārvatī’s marriage enables Tāraka’s future defeat
relations.note: She does not usually fight him; her son Skanda is born to kill him.

relations.myth: Kauśikī emerges from Pārvatī’s bodily sheath
relations.note: A radiant warrior goddess issues from Pārvatī while retaining a distinct identity.

relations.myth: Pārvatī becomes dark Kālikā after Kauśikī emerges
relations.note: The departing sheath leaves Pārvatī dark and called Kālikā.

relations.myth: Kālī emanates from the Goddess’s anger
relations.note: Other texts reverse the ontology and make Kālī an emanation of Pārvatī.
Later Śākta systems increasingly treat Kālī and Pārvatī as manifestations of one Devī.
Śaiva and Śākta taxonomies incorporate the warrior goddess as a form of Pārvatī.
Later Goddess theology links Caṇḍikā with Pārvatī while early narratives retain distinctions.
A formerly distinct Rudra-associated goddess becomes a standard name for Śiva’s wife.
Distinct fair, agricultural and regional goddess traditions become identified with Pārvatī.
The Vārāṇasī food-bestowing goddess is identified as a form of Pārvatī.
Some Śrīvidyā systems equate the autonomous tantric supreme Goddess with Pārvatī.
The major Kāñcīpuram goddess is theologically classified as Pārvatī.
Madurai’s autonomous sovereign goddess is later identified with Pārvatī.

relations.myth: Mīnākṣī marries Sundareśvara at Madurai
relations.note: Through identification with Mīnākṣī, Pārvatī marries Śiva’s local Madurai form.
Hampi’s local goddess is incorporated into Śaivism as Pārvatī.

relations.myth: Pampa marries Virūpākṣa at Hampi
relations.note: Through identification with Pampa, Pārvatī becomes consort of Śiva’s local form.
The Vārāṇasī goddess is incorporated into regional Pārvatī and Śakti theology.
The regional goddess is identified with Pārvatī as consort of a local Śiva.

relations.myth: Bhṛṅgi refuses to worship Pārvatī
relations.note: She merges with Śiva, but Bhṛṅgi persists by becoming skeletal or three-legged.

relations.myth: Rāvaṇa shakes Kailāsa and frightens Pārvatī
relations.note: She recoils or embraces Śiva while he pins Rāvaṇa beneath the mountain.

relations.myth: Umā supports boons granted to Kṛṣṇa
relations.note: Kṛṣṇa beholds the divine couple, and Umā independently grants or supports blessings.

relations.myth: Umā curses Earth after the gods interrupt her union
relations.note: She curses Earth to have many husbands after interruption of her union.
